10.1002_smll.76263: The electrocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is central to sustainable hydrogen production. Platinum (Pt) is widely regarded as the benchmark HER catalyst due to its near‐optimal catalytic properties. However, its scarcity and high cost severely constrain scalable deployment. Here, we demonstrate that structure‐induced interfacial electrostatic regulation enables platinum‐efficient HER while minimizing Pt loading. A one‐dimensional nanoensemble composed of Ag nanowires decorated with Pt nanoparticles integrates electronic hybridization, facet‐dependent charge accumulation, and directional charge transport to boost HER. The solid PtAgNW (S‐PtAgNW) nanoarchitecture containing only 15 wt.% Pt achieves the lowest overpotential of 290 mV at an ECSA‐normalized current density of 500 mA cm −2 with a Tafel slope of 42 mV dec −1 . It delivers a Pt‐normalized hydrogen production rate of ∼50 mol g Pt −1 h −1 at ∼93% Faradaic efficiency, representing a >6‐fold enhancement over its hollow counterpart despite the latter possessing higher Pt loading and similar interfacial chemistry. Mechanistic analysis reveals that Ag‐to‐Pt electronic coupling and facet redistribution toward Ag(111) enhance electron accumulation under bias, strengthening the interfacial electrostatic environment that governs proton‐electron coupling. These findings establish interfacial electrostatic regulation, rather than Pt loading or intrinsic catalyst chemistry alone, as an important determinant of efficient HER.
10.1021_acsenergylett.6c00158: Membrane-electrode assemblies utilize ionomer-coated electrocatalysts to achieve facile ion transport. Consequently, isolation of intrinsic catalyst kinetics from measured polarization curves is challenging, as the properties of the catalyst and ionomer both affect the measurements. Here, we employ a Pt microelectrode coated by a thin perfluorosulfonic acid (PFSA) layer to measure polarization curves for the hydrogen oxidation reaction/hydrogen evolution reaction (HER/HOR). Intrinsic electrode kinetics are isolated by theoretical analysis of the local catalyst microenvironment, accounting for mass transport and thermodynamics. The observed enhancements in HER and HOR rates with increasing relative humidity (RH) at the working electrode are attributable to two competing factors: the decrease in activity of H + in the ionomer and the dominant decrease in the water reorganization energy in the Marcus–Hush–Chidsey representation of HER/HOR kinetics. The increase in intrinsic rate with increasing RH is attributed to increased H + transfer dynamics resulting from reduced confinement of water within the subnanometer water layer between the catalyst and ionomer as RH increases.
